desc:
Some numbers can be written as a sum of consecutive positive integers, sometimes in several ways. Count the ways to write n as a sum of one or more consecutive positive integers. A single term (n itself) counts as one way. Two ways are different when their first term or their number of terms differs.

n = 5  -> 2   (5, and 2 + 3)
n = 8  -> 1   (only 8)
n = 9  -> 3   (9, 4 + 5, 2 + 3 + 4)
n = 15 -> 4   (15, 7 + 8, 4 + 5 + 6, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5)
hints: A run of k terms starting at a has sum k * a + k(k - 1) / 2. Try expressing a in terms of n and k.
Multiply the sum by 2: 2n = k * (2a + k - 1). So the run length k is one factor of 2n, and the other factor is determined by it.
The two factors have opposite parity, and each valid pair corresponds to one odd divisor of n. Count the odd divisors.
editorial: A run of k terms starting at a sums to k * a + k(k - 1) / 2. Doubling gives 2n = k * m with m = 2a + k - 1. Because a is at least 1, m is larger than k; and because m - k + 1 = 2a is even, k and m have opposite parity. Conversely, any factorization 2n = k * m with k < m and opposite parity gives a valid run with a = (m - k + 1) / 2 ≥ 1. So the ways correspond one-to-one with the factorizations of 2n into two factors of opposite parity.

Write n = 2e * o with o odd. The even factor must carry all the powers of two, so the odd factor is an odd divisor d of o, and the pair is {d, 2n / d}. Each odd divisor gives exactly one way, so the answer is the number of odd divisors of n. Remove the factors of 2 and count the divisors of the odd part by trial division up to its square root, which costs O(sqrt n).
